issuer: South Carolina Advisory Committee on Standards of Judicial Conduct (Supreme Court of South Carolina)
title: Advisory Opinion No. 01-2026: Propriety of a probate judge: 1) presenting a scholarship to a local student; 2) presenting a donation check to a charity.
text:
ADVISORY COMMITTEE
ON STANDARDS OF JUDICIAL CONDUCT
OPINION NO. 1 - 2026
RE:
Propriety of a probate judge: 1) presenting a scholarship to a local student; 2) presenting a
donation check to a charity.
FACTS
A probate judge is also the President of The South Carolina Association of Countywide
Elected Executives (SCACEE) until April 2026. SCACEE gives out a $1,000 scholarship to one
student who attends school in the President’s home county.  There is a committee of SCACEE
board members who will review the applications and pick a winner. The judge has no part,
involvement, or input on who is chosen to receive the scholarship. The judge inquires as to whether
the judge may present the $1,000 check to the winner.
The judge is also the current President of the South Carolina Association of Probate Judges
(SCAPJ) until October 2026.  According to the SCAPJ bylaws, a $200 donation is made to a
charity of the outgoing President’s choosing. The judge inquires as to whether the judge may
present the $200 donation to the charitable organization.
CONCLUSION
A probate judge may present both a scholarship check to a local student and a donation to
a charitable organization.
OPINION
Canon 2 (A) of the Code of Judicial Conduct requires that a judge conduct himself at all
times in a manner that promotes public confidence in the integrity and impartiality of the judiciary.
However, a judge may serve on organizations devoted to the improvement of the law, the legal

system or the administration of justice and with educational, religious, charitable, fraternal or civic
organizations not conducted for profit.
In Opinion 1-2025 we found that a circuit court judge could serve on the scholarship
selection committee for an affiliate organization of the National Association for Legal
Professionals. The affiliate awards annually a $1,500 scholarship to a deserving student who is
enrolled in a college, university, or tech school pursuing an undergraduate degree in Legal Studies
or seeking a Paralegal Certificate. Applying Canon 4(C)(3), we found that service on the
committee was permissible.  See also, Opinion 13-2000 (Circuit Court judge could serve on a
selection committee for a scholarship given at the University of South Carolina School of Law).
Here, the judge is not on the selection committee but would simply present the award on
behalf of the SCACEE. We conclude that such a presentation would not be prohibited by the
Canons.
The second inquiry by the judge is similar to the first. According to the SCAPJ bylaws, a
$200 donation is made to a charity of the outgoing President’s choosing. The judge is not engaging
in any fundraising efforts, but would merely be making a charitable donation on behalf of SCAPJ,
albeit an organization of the judge’s choice.  Since Canon 4C(3) allows a judge to be involved
with charitable organizations, we see no barrier to the judge presenting a donation to the charity
of his/her choice.
s/Usha Jeffries Bridges
USHA JEFFRIES BRIDGES, CHAIR
s/William H. Seals, Jr.
WILLIAM H. SEALS, JR.
s/Ariail E. King
Feb. 12, 2026
ARIAIL E. KING

issuer: South Carolina Advisory Committee on Standards of Judicial Conduct (Supreme Court of South Carolina)
title: Advisory Opinion No. 02-2026: Probate judge seeks opinion as to: 1) whether a probate judge may inquire into an attorney-fiduciary’s compliance with the rules; 2) when reporting obligations may be triggered; 3) proper judicial procedure to protect estate assets.
text:
ADVISORY COMMITTEE
ON STANDARDS OF JUDICIAL CONDUCT
OPINION NO. 2 - 2026
RE:
Probate judge seeks opinion as to: 1) whether a probate judge may inquire into an attorney­
fiduciary’s compliance with the rules; 2) when reporting obligations may be triggered; 3)
proper judicial procedure to protect estate assets.
FACTS
A Probate Judge has been presented with repeated fiduciary appointments involving an
attorney who drafted the underlying estate planning documents. This attorney names
himself/herself as Personal Representative or Trustee in wills and trusts he/she prepared for
decedents. In one estate, the beneficiaries expressed confusion or concern regarding the attorney's
dual role and the substantial fiduciary fees assessed, several of which have exceeded $100,000. In
another estate, the Court is concerned that a potential malpractice claim may exist against the same
attorney for drafting errors.
The Court is aware that Rule 1.8, Comment [8] of the South Carolina Rules of
Professional Conduct permits such appointments only where the attorney complies with Rule 1.7
by fully disclosing the conflict and advising the client of reasonable alternatives. Because these
instruments were executed prior to death, the Court has no record establishing whether such
disclosures and informed consent were obtained.
The Probate Judge seeks guidance on the following:(l) whether a Probate Judge has a duty
under the South Carolina Code of Judicial Conduct  to inquire into an attorney-fiduciary's
compliance with Rules 1.7 and 1.8 prior to appointment or approval of fees; (2) at what point a
recurring pattern of such appointments, combined with beneficiary concerns, triggers a reporting
obligation under Canon 3D(2) or Rule 2.15; and (3) the proper judicial procedure to protect estate
assets and beneficiaries while maintaining impartiality.

CONCLUSION
A probate judge may inquire into an attorney-fiduciary’s compliance with the rules. The
judge’s remaining questions are not within this Committee’s purview and thus, we cannot answer.
OPINION
Canon 3B(2) states that “[a] judge shall be faithful to the law and maintain professional
competence in it. Canon 3 also addresses judicial appointments (which includes the appointment
of counsel):
A judge shall not make unnecessary appointments. A judge shall exercise the
power of appointment impartially and on the basis of merit. A judge shall avoid
nepotism and favoritism. A judge shall not approve compensation of appointees
beyond the fair value of services rendered.
Canon 3C(4) (emphasis added). We read these sections, in addition to S.C. Code Ann. §  62-3­
203(e)(2), 1 to mean that the judge has the discretion to inquire into attorney-fiduciary’s
compliance with Rule 1.7 and 1.82 prior to appointment as a personal representative or approval
of fees.
As to the second question as when a reporting obligation, this Committee cannot opine.
We do note that Canon 3D(2) states:
A judge who receives information indicating a substantial likelihood that a lawyer
has committed a violation of the Rules of Professional Conduct contained in Rule
407, SCACR, should take appropriate action. A judge having knowledge that a
lawyer has committed a violation of the Rules of Professional Conduct that raises
a substantial question as to the lawyer's honesty, trustworthiness or fitness as a
lawyer in other respects shall inform the appropriate authority.
The Commentary to that section states:
1 This code section governs priority among persons seeking appointment as personal representative
and states that no personal is qualified to serve if the court finds unsuitable.
2 These are contained within the Rules of Professional Conduct, Rule 407, SCACR.
2

Appropriate action may include direct communication with the judge or lawyer who
has committed the violation, other direct action if available, and reporting the
violation to the appropriate authority or other agency or body.
However, we cannot advise a judge as to how many appointments or when the judge has sufficient
knowledge to take action under this Canon.
Likewise, we cannot advise as the proper judicial procedure to protect assets and
beneficiaries while maintaining impartiality. This is something the judge must determine based on
the facts, probate law and procedure, our ethical rules, and the judge’s own discretion.
s/Usha Jeffries Bridges
USHA JEFFRIES BRIDGES, CHAIR
s/William H. Seals, Jr.
WILLIAM H. SEALS, JR.
s/Ariail E. King
Feb. 12, 2026
ARIAIL E. KING
3

issuer: South Carolina Advisory Committee on Standards of Judicial Conduct (Supreme Court of South Carolina)
title: Advisory Opinion No. 03-2026: Propriety of a family court judge attending a dinner hosted by a law firm at an annual legal conference.
text:
ADVISORY COMMITTEE
ON STANDARDS OF JUDICIAL CONDUCT
OPINION NO. 3 - 2026
RE:
Propriety of a family court judge attending a dinner hosted by a law firm at an annual legal
conference.
FACTS
Every year the South Carolina Association for Justice (“SCAJ,” formerly known as the
South Carolina Trial Lawyers Association), has an annual conference in August at Hilton Head.
During the conference, some of the larger law firms host dinners. The firms generally will arrange
transportation to and from the restaurant and pay for dinner and drinks for their invited guest.
Guests will generally include the attorneys of the hosting firm, along with other attorneys that
practice in the same area of law or who have referred cases to the firm. In addition, certain
members of the General Assembly and/or Judiciary are invited to attend various dinners.  Usually,
the judges invited will be judges before which the lawyers of the host firm regularly appear.
Each year, there have been judges in attendance at certain dinners; however, some judges
have expressed concerns that allowing the law firm to pay for such dinner could be a problem for
the bench.  In addition, there has been a growing concern that even if it is appropriate to accept the
dinner, the judge must disclose the cost of the judge’s meal, drinks, and transportation on the
judge’s annual report.  The inquiring judge requests an opinion as to: 1) Whether a judge may
attend a dinner hosted by a law firm that employs lawyers who appear before the judge? 2) If the
judge can attend such dinner, must the judge disclosure the cost of the dinner on the judge’s annual
financial disclosure?

CONCLUSION
A family court judge may attend a dinner hosted by a law firm at an annual legal
convention.
OPINION
Canon 2 (A) of the Code of Judicial Conduct requires that a judge conduct himself at all times in
a manner that promotes public confidence in the integrity and impartiality of the judiciary.
However, a judge should not become isolated from the society in which he lives. Commentary,
Canon 4 (A). In Opinion 32-1994, this Committee addressed this issue, stating: “[j]udges cannot
be expected to sever all ties with society, including attending social occasions.”
In various opinions we have found that a judge can host a party or reception. See, Opinion
No. 17-1995 (permitting a judge to give a reception to thank friends in the community for allowing
him to serve them as an elected official); Opinion 10-1997 (judge could host a reception for city
employees and elected officials to express his appreciation); Opinion 07-2003 (family court judge
could host a reception for attorneys in the judicial circuit in which the judge presides, in order to
allow local lawyers and court personnel to meet on a non-work-related basis); and Opinion 1-2016
(judge and attorney son permitted to host a party for all judges attending the State Bar convention).
In addition, Canon 4 addresses gifts to judges and does allow a judge to accept “ordinary social
hospitality,” Canon 4D(5)(c).
While these opinions focus on the judge as host, they all involve a judge being able to
partake in social occasions, including ones that involve attorneys. Furthermore, in Op. 1-2016,
one of the hosts was an attorney who presumably appeared before the judges who would attend
the party. Thus, we see no violation of the Canons by allowing a judge to attend a dinner hosted
by a law firm at the SCAJ convention, even if some of the attorney dinner guests will appear
before the judge.
2

As to whether the judge must disclose the cost of the dinner and transportation on t

he
judge’s annual report, we have no opinion. “The purpose of the Committee shall be to render
written advisory opinions to inquiring judges concerning the propriety of contemplated judicial
and nonjudicial conduct.” Rule 503, SCACR. The Commentary to Canon 4D(5)(a)-(d) states
that:
A gift to a judge, or to a member of the judge's family living in the judge's
household, that is excessive in value raises questions about the judge's impartiality
and the integrity of the judicial office and might require disqualification of the judge
where disqualification would not otherwise be required.

The only monetary limitation discussed in the Canons states that a judge can accept:
any other gift, bequest, favor or loan, only if:  the donor is not a party or other
person who has come or is likely to come or whose interests have come or are likely
to come before the judge;  and, if its value exceeds $150.00, the judge reports it in
the same manner as the judge reports compensation in Section 4H[.]

Canon 4D(5)(e). In other words, “ordinary social hospitality” is different than any other
“gift, bequest, favor or loan” and not necessarily subject to the $150 limit. Thus, the judge
must use his or her discretion in determining whether a gift of ordinary social hospitality
is excessive. We also note that in Ethics Advisory Opinion 16-03, which addressed the
propriety of giving gifts to a new judge, that Committee stated:
The dollar value of the gift is not, by itself, determinative of the ethical inquiry.
There is, for example, no per se rule that a gift worth less than $150 is permissible
or that a gift worth more than $150 is impermissible. The dollar value of a gift is
relevant only in relation to the totality of the circumstances, including the nature
and duration of the relationship, the norms and customs of the community, the
number of lawyers contributing to the gift, and the nature of their practices.
s/Usha Jeffries Bridges
USHA JEFFRIES BRIDGES, CHAIR
s/William H. Seals, Jr.
WILLIAM H. SEALS, JR.
3

s/Ariail E. King
Feb. 12, 2026
ARIAIL E. KING
4

issuer: South Carolina Advisory Committee on Standards of Judicial Conduct (Supreme Court of South Carolina)
title: Advisory Opinion No. 04-2026: Propriety of a full-time magistrate engaging in employment as a hospitality driver on the judge’s personal time off.
text:
ADVISORY COMMITTEE
ON STANDARDS OF JUDICIAL CONDUCT

OPINION NO.  4 - 2026

RE:
Propriety of a full-time magistrate engaging in employment as a hospitality driver on the

judge’s personal time off.
FACTS

A magistrate court judge holds court in the jurisdictional district of the judge’s County or
judicial rotations through both Bond Court and/or Central Traffic Court.  The daily work schedule
is designed to accommodate rotating assignments first and then to fill the gaps by scheduling
criminal and civil hearings within the judge’s own courtroom that will not conflict with these other
courts.  Beyond court hearings, the judge is available to needs of local law enforcement agencies,
as well as the daily flow of “walk-in” business.

Once the administrative schedule is set and the judge’s judicial duties are confirmed, the
judge identifies days in which to take personal time off (“vacation days”).  While on some vacation
days the judge may simply stay at home or travel for pleasure, the judge may also engage in
secondary employment as a hospitality driver.

The job description of a hospitality driver in  this circumstance is simple.  The company
that judge would work with is in Florida. The company services multiple events across the United
States throughout the year by managing the transportation needs for their clients.  Transportation
is usually provided in full size SUV’s to and from events, restaurants, hotels and airports.  The
judge will not accept assignments in South Carolina and Georgia (located near the judge’s home
County) so as to avoid any potential conflicts.  Once the judge’s court schedule is confirmed and
a driving assignment is made, the judge will make the request to the Chief Magistrate and County
Administrator for the time away from the office to include the scope of travel regarding the basic
information of dates and times away.

CONCLUSION

A full-time magistrate judge may use personal time off to engage in employment as a
hospitality driver.

OPINION

Canon 4D(3) allows a judge to ”serve as an officer, director, manager, general partner,
advisor or employee of a business entity if that service does not conflict with the judge's judicial
duties, create the appearance of impropriety or otherwise violate any provision of this Code.”
(emphasis added). The judge would specifically only engage in such employment on days in which
the judge has personal time off, and therefore it would not interfere with the judge’s judicial duties.

This Committee is aware of the Supreme Court administrative order which states:
Chief Judges and Associate Chief Judges for Administrative Purposes, as well as
all other County magistrates, who are designated as full-time, are prohibited from
engaging in outside employment, judicial or otherwise, during the hours of 9:00
a.m. to 5:00 p.m., Monday through Friday unless authorized in writing by their
respective County governing body and approved by Court Administration.

Admin. Order, December 20, 2024, (emphasis in original).  However, since the judge will only be
engaging in employment during vacation days, and will otherwise be performing judicial duties
Monday-Friday, 9 a.m. – 5 p.m., we do not believe this order prevents the judge from employment
as a hospitality driver.

In addition, the judge will avoid any assignments in South Carolina or Georgia, so as to
limit any potential conflicts. Thus, we see no bar to this limited, nonjudicial employment.

s/Usha Jeffries Bridges

USHA JEFFRIES BRIDGES, CHAIR

s/William H. Seals, Jr.

WILLIAM H. SEALS, JR.

s/Ariail E. King
Feb. 12, 2026

ARIAIL E. KING

issuer: South Carolina Advisory Committee on Standards of Judicial Conduct (Supreme Court of South Carolina)
title: Advisory Opinion No. 05-2026: Propriety of a full-time magistrate sponsoring an event for the South Carolina Bar Foundation.
text:
ADVISORY COMMITTEE
ON STANDARDS OF JUDICIAL CONDUCT
OPINION NO. 5 - 2026
RE:
Propriety of a full-time magistrate sponsoring an event for the South Carolina Bar
Foundation.
FACTS
The South Carolina Bar Foundation (“the Foundation”) is a charitable organization that
has, since 1971 granted millions of dollars to law-related organizations across the State. The
Foundation provides funding for three primary categories of law-related nonprofits:
Administration of Justice, Civil Legal Aid and Law-Related Education.  Recent grant recipients
include: Charleston Legal Access (which expands access to justice by offering affordable legal
services for moderate to low-income citizens); The SC Supreme Court Historical Society (which
preserves and promotes the history of the state’s highest court, to help the public understand its
role); Upstate Medical Legal Partnership (which provides free legal help to low income patients);
and ABA Free Legal Answers (a national virtual clinic that allows eligible individuals to post legal
questions and receive answers from volunteer attorneys).
The Foundation hosts an event called “Cocktails in the Courtyard” in which local attorneys
and their guests attend to enjoy conversation, to make connections with other lawyers, and to learn
more about the Foundation. The judge inquires as to whether it is proper for him or her to be one
of the sponsor’s of the event.
CONCLUSION
A full-time magistrate may be a sponsor for a South Carolina Bar Foundation event.

OPINION
Canon 4B of the  Code of Judicial Conduct states that “[a] judge may speak, write, lecture,
teach and participate in other extra-judicial activities concerning the law, the legal system,
the administration of justice and non-legal subjects, subject to the requirements of this Code.
(emphasis added). Canon 4C(3) states that “[a] judge may serve as an officer, director, trustee or
non-legal advisor of an organization or governmental agency devoted to the improvement of the
law, the legal system or the administration of justice or of an educational, religious, charitable,
fraternal or civic organization not conducted for profit….”
The Foundation is a charitable organization focused on the legal system and making legal
services and legal education available to citizens of the State. Thus, we see no reason why a judge
should not be permitted to sponsor a Foundation event. With regard to whether the judge’s title
should be used in any materials listing sponsors, we do not believe this would be abusing the
prestige of office.  While South Carolina’s Code of Conduct does not specifically address this
issue, other states have. For example, New Hampshire’s Rule 3.7(A)(4) states that a judge is not
prohibited from:
appearing or speaking at, receiving an award or other recognition at, being featured
on the program of, and permitting his or her title to be used in connection with
an event of [a religious, charitable, fraternal, or civic] organization or entity,
but if the event serves a fund-raising purpose, the judge may participate only
if the event concerns the law, the legal system, or the administration of
justice[.]
(emphasis added).1 We are persuaded by the logic of that rule. Here, the Foundation is both
charitable and concerns the legal system and administration of justice, so we do not believe that it
1 Indiana has a similar rule allowing the use of a judicial title. See Ind. Code of Judicial Conduct,
Rule 3.7(A)(4).
2

would be improper for the judge’s title to be used in any materials regarding the sponsors of the
event. However, the judge is reminded that judges should not personally participate in the
solicitation of funds to the Foundation except for family members or other judges over which the
inquiring judge has no supervisory authority.

s/Usha Jeffries Bridges

USHA JEFFRIES BRIDGES, CHAIR

s/William H. Seals, Jr.

WILLIAM H. SEALS, JR.

s/Ariail E. King
April 7, 2026

ARIAIL E. KING

3

issuer: South Carolina Advisory Committee on Standards of Judicial Conduct (Supreme Court of South Carolina)
title: Advisory Opinion No. 06-2026: Propriety of a special referee in a residential foreclosure action also serving as the closing attorney for the third party bidder who purchased the property at the foreclosure sale.
text:
ADVISORY COMMITTEE
ON STANDARDS OF JUDICIAL CONDUCT
OPINION NO. 6 - 2026
RE:
Propriety of a special referee in a residential foreclosure action also serving as the closing
attorney for the third party bidder who purchased the property at the foreclosure sale.
FACTS
A lawyer recently received an Order of Reference to act as a special referee1 in a residential
foreclosure action. The case went to a sale and was purchased by a third-party bidder. The special
referee was asked by the bidder to serve as closing attorney for this parcel. The special referee
declined, feeling that there was a conflict of interest. The special referee is aware that others have
acted as special referee and closing attorney for the same property – whether the special
referee/master conducted the closing or another attorney in the special referee’s firm did so.
Though the special referee has turned down the request to close the transaction, the judge would
consider handling such closings in the future if it is not a conflict of interest.
CONCLUSION
A special referee in a residential foreclosure action should not act as the closing attorney
for the third-party bidder who purchased the property at the foreclosure sale.
1 In the “Application of the Code of Judicial Conduction” section of Rule 501, it states: “Anyone,
whether or not a lawyer, who is an officer of the unified judicial system and who performs
judicial functions, including an officer such as a magistrate, master-in-equity or special referee,
is a judge within the meaning of this Code.” (emphasis added). The special referee has also
requested an opinion from South Carolina Bar as to whether there is a violation of the Rules of
Professional Conduct for lawyers. In this opinion, we only address the judge’s inquiry as to
whether any of the Code of Judicial Conduct would be violated and we do not address the Rules
of Professional Conduct.

s/Usha Jeffries Bridges

USHA JEFFRIES BRIDGES, CHAIR

s/William

 H.

 Seals,

 Jr.

WILLIAM H. SEALS, JR.

s/Ariail E. King
March 25, 2026

ARIAIL E. KING
2

OPINION
Canon 2 requires a judge to act at all times in a manner that promotes public confidence in
the integrity and impartiality of the judiciary. Canon 2B states “a judge shall not lend the prestige
of judicial office to advance the private interests of the judge or others; nor shall a judge convey
or permit others to convey the impression that they are in a special position to influence the judge.”
A special referee is a judicial role and he/she must abide by the Canons. If the foreclosure
results in a sale, the closing attorney or firm will receive income as a result.  The special referee’s
service (or his/her firm’s service) as closing attorney for the same property in the foreclosure action
over which the special referee presided could lead to the appearance that the special referee ruled
in a specific way in order to generate revenue for himself/herself. In other words, we do not believe
that conduct conforms to Canon 2’s requirement that judges act “in a manner that promotes  public
confidence in the integrity and impartiality of the judiciary.” Moreover, it could appear that the
special referee is using judicial office to advance his/her own interests in violation of Canon 2B.
Thus, we think prudent court of action is for the special referee to decline to act as a closing
attorney for a third-party purchaser where the judge presided over the foreclosure that led to the
sale of the property.

issuer: South Carolina Advisory Committee on Standards of Judicial Conduct (Supreme Court of South Carolina)
title: Advisory Opinion No. 07-2026: Propriety of a circuit court judge conducting mediations or providing legal advice outside the State of South Carolina.
text:
ADVISORY COMMITTEE
ON STANDARDS OF JUDICIAL CONDUCT
OPINION NO. 7 - 2026
RE:
Propriety of a circuit court judge conducting mediations or providing legal advice outside
the State of South Carolina.
FACTS
A circuit court judge’s partner, who is not an attorney, owns a mediation firm. While the
mediation firm does have a physical office in South Carolina, it offers mediation services
throughout the United States and conducts many of them via Zoom.  Because all of the employees
of the firm have other full-time jobs, mediations are often scheduled on evenings or weekends,
outside of regular business hours. In addition, while lawyers typically engage in evaluative
mediation, the firm specializes in transformative mediation – mediation which encourages the
parties to come to an agreement themselves, and the mediator does not offer opinions as to the
strengths or weaknesses of the dispute. According to the judge, this can be done without identifying
the mediator as a judge or using the prestige of the office in any way.
The judge also inquires as to whether, if the judge is licensed in another state, he or she is
able to offer legal advice to citizens of that other state. While the judge acknowledges that he/she
could not have any semblance of a law practice, the judge asks whether he/she could serve as legal
advisor or consulting counsel for a business or its customers if that advice concerns the laws of
another state.
CONCLUSION
A circuit court judge may not serve as a mediator, even if the mediation conferences involve
litigants outside of South Carolina. A circuit court judge cannot serve as legal advisor or consulting

counsel for a business, even if that advice concerns the laws of another state, as it would constitute
the practice of law.
OPINION
Canon 4F states “[a] judge shall not act as an arbitrator or mediator or otherwise perform
judicial functions in a private capacity unless expressly authorized by law.” The only exception
allows a retired judge to act as an arbitrator or mediator and remain available for assignment as a
judge by the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court. Canon 4G states that a judge shall not practice
law. The only exception is that a “a judge may act pro se and may, without compensation, give
legal advice to and draft or review documents for a member of the judge's family.”
Neither the Canons nor the Commentary thereto allow for a judge to engage in mediation
outside of South Carolina or as a legal advisor to an out of state business.
Thus, we find that a full-time judge may not act as a mediator for litigants outside of South
Carolina (whether conducted in-person or via Zoom), even if the mediations would take place
outside of normal business hours. Similarly, we find that a circuit court judge cannot serve as a
legal advisor or consulting counsel for a business, even if that advice concerns the laws of another
state, as it would constitute the practice of law.
s/Usha Jeffries Bridges

USHA JEFFRIES BRIDGES, CHAIR
s/William H. Seals, Jr.
WILLIAM H. SEALS, JR.
Ariail E. King
April 23, 2026

ARIAIL E. KING
2

issuer: South Carolina Advisory Committee on Standards of Judicial Conduct (Supreme Court of South Carolina)
title: Advisory Opinion No. 08-2026: Propriety of a bond court judge predetermining bail before the defendant is brought before the court for a hearing.
text:
ADVISORY COMMITTEE
ON STANDARDS OF JUDICIAL CONDUCT

OPINION NO.  8 - 2026

RE:
Propriety of a bond court judge predetermining bail before the defendant is brought

before the court for a hearing.

FACTS

A municipal court judge inquires into the propriety of a bond court judge (such as a
ministerial recorder or other judicial officer who presides over pre-trial bond hearings following
an arrest) predetermining bail before the defendant is brought before the court for a hearing.

The judge notes that some municipal courts lack the facilities to conduct bond hearings on-
site, requiring their bond court judges to physically travel to the county detention facility and
conduct hearings through a glass partition in the booking area of the jail. Based on these
limitations, the judge inquires as to whether it is permissible for judges to pre-determine
defendants’ bail on account of paperwork efficiency.

S.C. Code §§ 17-15-30 and 22-5-510 outline what bond court judges may or must consider
in determining a pre-trial defendant’s bond, and much of that information—such as records of
convictions, flight risks, failure to appear, criminal records, and incident reports—can be reviewed
prior to the court session. However, critical information cannot be gained from these records alone.
Permissive factors such as a defendant’s family ties, employment, financial resources, character,
mental condition, and length of residence in the community are usually only ascertainable through
an actual hearing with the defendant.
2

The judge is concerned that the practice of pre-determining bonds may violate the Canons,
including, inter alia, the following:1
• Canon 1A, which requires that a judge “participate in establishing, maintaining and
enforcing high standards of conduct…”
• Canon 2A, which mandates that a judge “shall respect and comply with the law and shall
act at all times in a manner that promotes public confidence in the integrity and
impartiality of the judiciary.”
• Canon 3B(7), which guarantees that a judge “shall accord to every person who has a legal
interest in a proceeding, or that person’s lawyer, the right to be heard according to law.”
CONCLUSION

While a judge may review information about a defendant before a bond hearing, a judge
cannot predetermine bail under any circumstances.
OPINION

The inquiring judge is correct in that the Canons cited are applicable to bond hearings.
While a judge may review various records prior to the bond hearing, and may even consider a
range for bond, the judge must consider other factors that will only be presented at the hearing. If
the judge has predetermined bond and refuses to consider other factors at a bond hearing, the
defendant is not be afforded the right to be heard. 2

1 The judge is concerned that there may also be issues impacting procedural due process.

2 The Advisory Committee has been informed that South Carolina Court Administration actively
advises judges not to engage in this practice.
3

While this may create hardships for some municipal courts/judges, the Canons require
judges to establish, maintain and enforce “high standards of conduct….” Canon 1A.  Pre-
determining bond would clearly violate the standards of conduct in the Canons.

s/ Usha Jeffries Bridges

USHA JEFFRIES BRIDGES, CHAIR

s/William H. Seals, Jr.

WILLIAM H. SEALS, JR.

s/Ariail E. King
May 6, 2026

ARIAIL E. KING

issuer: South Carolina Advisory Committee on Standards of Judicial Conduct (Supreme Court of South Carolina)
title: Advisory Opinion No. 09-2026: Propriety of the spouse of a Family Court judge using social media to support the campaign of a family friend who is running for statewide office and/or attending campaign parties.
text:
ADVISORY COMMITTEE
ON STANDARDS OF JUDICIAL CONDUCT

OPINION NO.  9 - 2026

RE:
Propriety of the spouse of a Family Court judge using social media to support the

campaign of a family friend who is running for statewide office and/or attending

campaign parties.

FACTS

A friend and neighbor of  a Family Court Judge is running for statewide office. The judge’s
spouse wants to use his/her Facebook and Instagram pages to show support for their friend by
posting links to the friend’s websites; posting other messages of support; and “liking” posts of
others. The judge does not have a Facebook, Instagram, or any other social media account.
However, there are many photos of the judge on the spouse’s social media pages. There are no
photos of the judge in judicial robes, but there are some posts recognizing the judge’s judicial
position, such as a congratulatory post when the judge was first elected.  Many of the spouse’s
Facebook friends are aware of the judge’s position.

The judge inquires as to whether his/her spouse can utilize social media as described.  The
judge also inquires as to whether his/her spouse could attend parties for the friend, if not as a
contributor or host.
CONCLUSION

The spouse of a Family Court judge may use social media to support the campaign of a
family friend who is running for statewide office and also may attend campaign parties.
OPINION

While a judge or judicial candidate is specifically prohibited from certain political activities
under Canon 5, Rule 501, SCACR, the Canons do not specifically address the conduct of a judge's

family members. However, the Commentary to Canon 5A(3)(a) states "Although a judicial
candidate must encourage members of his or her family to adhere to the same standards of political
conduct in support of the candidate that apply to the candidate, family members are free to
participate in other political activity." In Opinion 33-2001, we determined that a judge's spouse is
free to contribute monetarily or volunteer in a political campaign as long as the judge's name is not
used in connection with the spouse's activities. We found that a judge’s spouse may not introduce
herself or himself as the spouse of a judge when soliciting funds or participating in door-to-door
campaigning and any financial contributions should not be made from a joint checking account.
Here, the judge’s spouse wants to use his/her social media pages to support their friend’s
campaign for statewide office. We find that the spouse may use these pages to post messages of
support or links to the friend/candidate’s website.  However, the spouse must ensure that his/her
page does not reference the judge’s position either in the biographical “About” section of the social
media page or in photographs.  As to attending campaign parties, the spouse is free to attend and
can contribute as long as the funds are not paid from a joint checking account
s/Usha Jeffries Bridges
USHA JEFFRIES BRIDGES, CHAIR
s/William H. Seals, Jr.
WILLIAM H. SEALS, JR.
Ariail E. King
May 8, 2026
ARIAIL E. KING

title: Advisory Opinion No. 10-2026: Propriety of a probate judge, who is on a Board of Trustees for an education group, attending a conference that will be paid for by one of the groups over which the Board of Trustees govern.
text:
ADVISORY COMMITTEE
ON STANDARDS OF JUDICIAL CONDUCT

OPINION NO.  10 - 2026

RE:
Propriety of a probate judge, who is on a Board of Trustees for an education group,

attending a conference that will be paid for by one of the groups over which the Board of

Trustees govern.

FACTS

A probate judge sits on the Board of Trustees (“the Board”) for an education group.  The
board governs a middle and high school (non-profit); a press division (for profit); and a university’s
collection of religious art and other infrastructure (non-profit). The press division sells educational
materials with a biblical world view.  The Board encourages each of the trustees to attend a Biblical
WorldView Conference in California, hosted by the press division, to better understand the
academic curriculum they produce.  The press division pays for the trustee to attend the conference
and airfare, hotel, and food for the trustee and this/her spouse. The education group and its
divisions do not ever come before the probate court in which the judge serves. The judge inquires
into the propriety of attending the conference under these circumstances.
CONCLUSION

A probate judge, as a member of a Board of Trustees for an education group, may attend
a conference that will be paid for by one of the groups over which the Board govern.
OPINION

 A judge must uphold the integrity and independence of the judiciary. Canon 1, SCACR
(Supp. 1998). Canon 2 further states that a judge must avoid all impropriety and appearance of
impropriety.  Canon 4C (3) permits a judge to serve as an officer, director, trustee of an educational,
religious, charitable, fraternal or civic organization.
2

Here, the judge is a trustee for an education group as permitted by Canon 4. The Board
intends to send the judge and his/her spouse to an out of state conference and will pay for all
expenses. We addressed a similar question in Opinion 5-2012. In that case, local circuit court
judges who preside in drug court wanted to attend a national training conference for drug court
and other types of remedial courts. The attendance fees for the judges’ attendance at the conference
would come from the county’s drug court fees.  We found the judges could attend.

In another opinion, Op. 9-1998, a magistrate has inquired into the propriety of attending a
conference hosted and financed by a local housing authority. The magistrate there handled
landlord-tenant matters involving this housing authority, although the cases were limited to
evictions. We noted that a judge should not attend any event at the expense of an  organization
which is likely to appear in his or her court. Canon 4(D)(5)(h).  However, the inquiring judge here
has indicated that the Board and its subdivisions does not appear before the Probate Court.

Thus, after reviewing the applicable Canons and our previous opinions, we find that
attendance at the conference at the expense of the press division of the Board is permissible.

s/Usha Jeffries Bridges

USHA JEFFRIES BRIDGES, CHAIR

s/William H. Seals, Jr.

WILLIAM H. SEALS, JR.

s/Ariail E. King

ARIAIL E. KING
May 4, 2026

title: Advisory Opinion No. 11-2026: A Probate Judge has recently become aware that a probate court employee is running for Probate Judge.  Another employee has posted on social media support for the candidate running for Probate Judge.
text:
ADVISORY COMMITTEE
ON STANDARDS OF JUDICIAL CONDUCT
OPINION NO.  11 - 2026
RE:
Propriety of probate court employees running for Probate Judge or publicly supporting
or endorsing a candidate running for Probate Judge.
FACTS
A Probate Judge has recently become aware that a probate court employee is running for
Probate Judge. Another employee has posted on social media support for the candidate running
for Probate Judge. The judge is concerned as to whether these acts are a violation of Rule 507,
SCACR, which prohibits employees of the Judicial Department from being a candidate in a
partisan election or participating in the political campaigns of others. The inquiring judge is
concerned that these two employees should be terminated for violating Rule 507.
CONCLUSION
Probate court employees are permitted to run for elective partisan office without first
resigning. In addition, probate court employees are not prohibited from endorsing candidates on
social media.
OPINION
Rule 507, SCACR, governs political activity of the judicial department. Section 1 of that
rule states that an employee or officer of the Judicial Department may not “[b]e a candidate for
elective office in a partisan election].” Rule 507, Sec. 1C. 1 The rule also states that an employee
or officer may not “[a]ctively participate in the campaign of any political party or candidate.”  Rule
1 According to S.C. Code § 14-23-30, the judges of the Probate Court are elected, by the
qualified electors of the respective counties for the term of four years. The elections are partisan.
See, S.C. Code § 7-11-10.
2
507, Sec. 1D. Section 2 of Rule 507 authorizes this Committee to “issue advisory opinions
concerning this rule in accordance with the procedures established in Rule 503, SCACR.”
However, it is not clear that probate court employees are South Carolina Judicial
Department (“SCJD”) employees. While probate courts are a part of the unified judicial system
under S.C. Code Ann. § 14-23-1010, their inclusion does not necessarily mean that probate court
employees are SCJD employees. See, Bank of New York v. Sumter County, 387 S.C. 147, 691
S.E.2d 473 (2010) (holding that, while master-in-equity courts are part of the unified judicial
system, masters-in-equity are not SCJD employees). In fact, the following factors would indicate
that probate court employees are county employees, not SCJD employees:
a.
Probate courts are funded by the counties. See S.C. Code Ann. § 14-23-1030 (“In
addition to the judge of probate, there shall be one or more associate judges of
probate in any county whose governing body appropriates the funds therefor.”); See
also S.C. Code Ann. § 14-23-1130 (“The governing body of each county shall
provide and the judge of probate shall keep the seal of the probate court, the
necessary office equipment of the probate court, and those books as are necessary
for keeping the records of the probate court […] In addition, the governing body of
each county shall provide office space and additional support personnel necessary
for the orderly conduct of the business of the probate court.”).
b.
Unlike their circuit and family counterparts, probate court judges cannot participate
in the judicial retirement system, S.C. Code Ann. § 9-8-10(16), and are not excluded
from SCRS, S.C. Code Ann. §9-1-10.
The Supreme Court maintains control over the probate courts (as it does the master-in­
equity courts), but this control is indicative of their inclusion in the unified judicial system, not an
employer/employee relationship. See, e.g., S.C. Code Ann. §14-23-1140 (“The Supreme Court
shall have the power by rule to regulate the practice, procedure, and conduct of business in the
courts of probate.”); see also S.C. Code Ann. § 14-23-1080 (in cases of recusal, “the Chief Justice
of the Supreme Court shall appoint a special judge to sit in the matter.”).
3
Some of our previous opinions have construed the class of “Judicial Department employees
and officers” under Rule 507, SCACR, more broadly than the Court construed that class in Bank
of New York v. Sumter County. Specifically, our past opinions have included magistrate’s clerks
as judicial department employees without discussion. See Re: Propriety of a Magistrate Courts
Clerk Running for the Elected Office of Mayor, Opinion No. 10-2016 (April 12, 2016) (advising
that the clerk could continue employment because the election is nonpartisan); Re: Propriety of a
Part-Time Magistrate’s Part-Time Clerk Running for the Elected Office of Town Council, Opinion
No. 21-2006 (August 6, 2006) (advising that a part-time magistrate’s clerk is prohibited from
running for the elected position of town council). These decisions appear to originate and cite
back to the April 15, 2004, advisory opinion. That opinion found that magistrate’s clerks, who are
hired, paid, and supervised by the county, were comparable to court reporters, who are hired, paid,
and supervised by SCJD for the purposes of Rule 507. Adv. Op. 8-2004.
After reviewing the Bank of New York v. Sumter County case, we have determined that
non-judge Probate Court employees are employed by the County and thus are not employees of
the SCJD.2 Therefore, the employee is permitted to run for Probate Judge without first resigning
his or her position.
In addition, with regard to the Facebook post supporting the employee-candidate, it appears
not to be active participation in a campaign but instead, serves as a public endorsement. As long
as the employee is not a staff attorney or law clerk who is not permitted to endorse a candidate,
the employee is permitted to endorse the candidate. 3
2 This finding means that, most likely, magistrate court employees are also not employees of
SCJD but, since the current inquiry does not include any issues involving the magistrate court,
we will reserve that discussion for the future.
3 Rule 506, SCACR, which governs the conduct of staff attorneys and law clerks, prohibits
public endorsement and speeches for political candidates.
4
s/Usha Jeffries Bridges
USHA JEFFRIES BRIDGES, CHAIR
s/William H. Seals, Jr.
WILLIAM H. SEALS, JR.
Ariail E. King
June 15, 2026
ARIAIL E. KING

title: Advisory Opinion No. 01-2025: Propriety of a Circuit Court judge serving on a board to award a small scholarship to student who is enrolled in a college, university, or tech school pursuing an undergraduate degree in Legal Studies or seeking a Paralegal Certificate.
text:
ADVISORY COMMITTEE
ON STANDARDS OF JUDICIAL CONDUCT
OPINION NO. 1 - 2025
RE:
Propriety of a Circuit Court judge serving on a board to award a small scholarship to student
who is enrolled in a college, university, or tech school pursuing an undergraduate degree
in Legal Studies or seeking a Paralegal Certificate.
FACTS
A Circuit Court Judge has been contacted by a member of Legal Staff Professionals of
South Carolina (“LSPSC”), a group of members who work in law firms and other legal entities as
administrative people. The organization is an affiliate of the National Association for Legal
Professionals.  The member is the chair of the 2025 Scholarship Committee. LSPSC awards
annually a $1,500 scholarship to a deserving student who is enrolled in a college,  university, or
tech school pursuing an undergraduate degree in Legal Studies or seeking a Paralegal Certificate.
The award will be made in April 2025 at the annual education conference.  The Scholarship
Committee is seeking three people to view applications and rank them: A judge, a teacher, and a
community leader.  The Scholarship Committee has asked the judge to participate.
The Scholarship Committee will send the judge the applications for review. The judge
would then rank them based on the criteria/qualifications. There are usually only a small number
of applications so the reviewing process would not interfere with the judge’s judicial duties.
CONCLUSION
A Circuit Court judge may serve on a selection committee for a scholarship given by the
LSPSC.
OPINION
A judge shall conduct all of the judge's extrajudicial activities so that they do not cast
reasonable doubt on the judge's capacity to act impartially as a judge. Rule 501, Canon 4(A) (1),

SCACR. A judge may serve as officer, director, trustee or non-legal advisor of an education
organization not conducted for profit. Rule 501, Canon 4(C)(3), SCACR. In Opinion 13-2000, we
addressed a similar question as the one presented here.  There, we found that a Circuit Court judge
could serve on a selection committee for a scholarship given at the University of South Carolina
School of Law. We determined that  the scholarship selection committee is a nonprofit educational
organization and thus the judge could serve. We see no reason to deviate from that logic here.
Thus, the inquiring judge may participate in the ranking of scholarship applications for the LSPSC.
s/Usha Jeffries Bridges
USHA JEFFRIES BRIDGES, CHAIR
s/William H. Seals, Jr.
WILLIAM H. SEALS, JR.
s/Ariail E. King
February 13, 2025
ARIAIL E. KING
